stall.lastCandidateQuestion:
My recommendation is to raise menu prices first.

The reason is sizing. COGS went from 42 to 58 points of revenue, and prices haven't moved in two years, so the company absorbed all of it. A price increase is the only lever that acts fast and scales across all 200 locations — supplier renegotiation takes months and menu reengineering takes longer. Roughly, pushing through enough price to recover even half the 16 points would put margin back in the mid-teens.

Risks: specialty coffee customers may be price sensitive, and volume could drop. Also competitors may not have raised prices.

Next steps: test an increase in a handful of markets and watch transaction volume — do we have transaction counts by store? Then start supplier negotiations in parallel, since that's slower but durable.

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.
I'm not sure what you mean — do you want me to guess why profits went down?

No guessing. I'd like you to lay out how you would structure the problem, meaning the areas you would investigate and why. Take a minute if you need it, and you can also ask me clarifying questions first.
hmm, I'm not sure. What kind of areas do you mean?
Take your time. The question on the table is how you would break this profit decline into parts so you can find the root cause. Walk me through how you'd organize your investigation.
I'm stuck, sorry. I don't really know where to start.
That's okay. Start from the one thing we know: profit fell while revenue grew. What basic pieces make up profit, and which of them would you want to look at first?
hmm... revenue and profit? I'm not sure, sorry.
Let's simplify. Profit is what's left after something comes out of revenue. What are the two ways a profit margin can fall?
I guess... revenue or something else? I really don't know.
Okay. You've got revenue as one piece, so revenue is a good place to start. What is the other piece, the thing that gets subtracted from revenue to leave profit?
hmm, I want to say expenses? But I'm not sure how that helps.

Yes, expenses. Revenue has grown, so the pressure is on the cost side, and that's where we'll look. Here's the cost data. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Which of these costs moved the most?
COGS moved the most — it went from 42% to 58%, so that's 16 points of revenue. Labor didn't move at all, and overhead only went up 2 points. So most of the margin drop is coming from COGS.
Okay. COGS is the biggest mover, so what would you want to know next to understand why it rose?
I guess what's actually inside COGS? Like coffee beans versus milk versus cups — is there a breakdown of that line? And did our menu prices change at all over the two years?

Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. Menu prices have not changed in two years. Which of these would you quantify first to explain the COGS increase, and how would you do it?

I'd probably start with the "other inputs" since they're the bigger share — 75% of COGS versus 25% for beans. If that 75% went up 37.5%, that's 0.75 × 37.5% = about 28% increase in COGS on its own, holding beans flat.

And since prices never changed, none of that got passed to customers, so it all hits the margin.

I'd still want to know what beans did over the same period, since that's the other quarter.

Walk me through the translation from that 28% to the margin. COGS was 42% of revenue two years ago, and 28% is a share of COGS. You asked about that — Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. How many points of revenue does it represent?

Let me do it in points of revenue. Old COGS was 42 points. Beans were 25% of that, so 10.5 points, and other inputs 75%, so 31.5 points.

Beans up 40%: 10.5 × 1.4 = 14.7, so +4.2 points.
Other inputs up 37.5%: 31.5 × 1.375 = 43.3, so +11.8 points.

Total new COGS = 14.7 + 43.3 = 58 points, which matches the 58% you gave me. So the increase is about 16 points of revenue, with roughly 12 from other inputs and 4 from beans.

That 16 plus the 2 points of overhead is about 18, which is the whole 24% to 6% drop.
Okay. Here's the cost structure over time. What does it tell you, and what's the main insight you'd take from it?

It's a steady slide, not a one-time shock. COGS goes 42 to 50 to 58, so about 8 points a year, two years running. Labor is flat at 22 the whole time, overhead creeps up 1 point a year, and profit falls 24 to 15 to 6, which is roughly 9 points a year.

Main insight is that essentially all of the damage is COGS, and it's been happening consistently rather than suddenly. And with menu prices unchanged for two years, the company has absorbed every bit of that input inflation itself. If it continues at this pace, profit goes negative next year.
Understood. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could Brew & Bean do to reverse this decline? Give me your ideas in an organized way.

I'll try to group them. On the revenue side, the obvious one is raising menu prices, since they haven't moved in two years while inputs went up almost 40%. Even a modest increase passes some of that through.

On the cost side, they could renegotiate supplier contracts or lock in longer-term pricing on beans and dairy so they're not exposed to every swing. With 200 locations they probably have some buying power.

They could also look at the menu itself — push items that use less of the expensive inputs, or adjust portion sizes.

And overhead is drifting up 1 point a year, which is smaller but worth a look.

I'd want to know how price-sensitive their customers are before recommending a big price increase, though.
Okay. Of the ideas you've grouped, which would you prioritize first, and why? Give me your recommendation to the CEO.

My recommendation is to raise menu prices first.

The reason is sizing. COGS went from 42 to 58 points of revenue, and prices haven't moved in two years, so the company absorbed all of it. A price increase is the only lever that acts fast and scales across all 200 locations — supplier renegotiation takes months and menu reengineering takes longer. Roughly, pushing through enough price to recover even half the 16 points would put margin back in the mid-teens.

Risks: specialty coffee customers may be price sensitive, and volume could drop. Also competitors may not have raised prices.

Next steps: test an increase in a handful of markets and watch transaction volume — do we have transaction counts by store? Then start supplier negotiations in parallel, since that's slower but durable.

You said recovering half the 16 points would put margin back in the mid-teens. Walk me through that. Then tell me how a price increase actually gets you there. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. I don't have data on that.

Half of 16 is 8 points, and current margin is 6, so 6 + 8 = 14, which is what I meant by mid-teens.

On how a price increase gets there — it's actually a bit different from just subtracting costs. If costs stay flat in dollars and I raise prices, revenue goes up and the cost lines shrink as a percentage. Costs today are 94 points. If I raised prices 10% with no volume loss, costs become 94/1.10 ≈ 85 points of the new revenue, so margin goes to about 15%. That's roughly the same answer.

And the ticket data is useful — the $6.20 to $6.80 came from more items per visit, not price, so none of that was pass-through. It also suggests customers are willing to spend more, which is mildly encouraging for a price move.
Okay. Your own sizing assumes no volume loss, and the data says nothing about how customers respond to price. If a 10% increase did cost you transactions, how would that change your recommendation?

It would depend on how much volume we lost. Rough logic: at 10% higher prices, if volume fell a lot, revenue could end up flat or down, and COGS is variable so it falls with volume too — but labor and overhead are partly fixed, so those would get worse as a percent of revenue.

Quick sense of it: gross margin today is only about 42 cents on the dollar after COGS, so we don't have much cushion. If we lost, say, 10% of transactions, we'd roughly break even on revenue and the fixed costs would still hurt us.

So I'd soften the recommendation — pilot it in a few markets rather than rolling out chain-wide, and start supplier renegotiation at the same time rather than treating it as the slower backup.
Walk me through that break-even claim. If prices rise 10% and transactions fall 10%, how do you get to roughly breaking even on profit, not just revenue?

Let me actually redo it, I think I conflated revenue and profit.

Start at 100 of revenue: COGS 58, labor 22, overhead 14, profit 6.

Price +10%, volume −10%: revenue = 100 × 1.1 × 0.9 = 99, so basically flat, that part was right.

COGS is variable, so it moves with volume, not price: 58 × 0.9 = 52.2. Labor and overhead I'm treating as fixed, so still 36.

Total costs = 88.2. Profit = 99 − 88.2 = 10.8 points.

So profit actually improves from 6 to about 11, not break-even. My earlier claim was wrong — I was looking at revenue and assuming profit followed. The reason it holds up is that the price increase is pure margin while the volume loss only takes variable cost with it.

That makes me more comfortable with the price move, though I'd still pilot it.
We'll stop there. Thanks for working through the case — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Practice opening every profitability case independently with a 30-second structure: restate the objective, split profit into revenue (price × volume, mix) and costs (COGS, labor, overhead), then state a hypothesis about which bucket holds the answer. Here you needed three escalating hints and a directive rescue before you could begin, even though your later analysis was strong.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue
Other inputs as points of revenue today = 31.5 points two years ago × 1.375 = 43.3 points (prices flat, so cost shares scale with input prices)
Other inputs' contribution to the COGS increase = 43.3 − 31.5 = 11.8 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
